questions.prompt: Why is a black hole black?
options: It is covered in dark dust that absorbs light
Inside the event horizon, escape requires moving faster than light — so no light can ever get out
It is simply in a dark part of the galaxy
It is a shadow cast by another star
questions.explanation: Light travels at the fastest speed there is, but escape from inside the horizon would need to go even faster. No light returns, so the region looks black.
questions.misconception: 'Black' naturally reads as 'an object that absorbs light, like a black shirt' — but the black here is a missing ability to leave, not a color of the surface.

questions.prompt: What exactly is the event horizon?
options: The solid surface of the black hole
The spherical boundary where escape speed reaches light speed — the point of no return
The edge of the galaxy around the hole
A ring of fire made of burning gas
questions.explanation: It is a boundary in space, not a surface: inside it, nothing — matter, light, signals — can ever cross back out. It only appears as a sphere because gravity acts that way in all directions.
questions.misconception: We picture a hard ball in space, but the horizon is a geometric threshold — like the point past which you cannot climb back up a hill with a bicycle, drawn in the sky around a collapsed core.

questions.prompt: In a real photo of a black hole, what are you actually seeing?
options: The black hole itself, glowing faintly
Its shadow against the glowing accretion disk, with the light behind it lensed into rings and arcs
The singularity through a window
A mirror of the galaxy
questions.explanation: The hole emits nothing, so the image is the shadow it casts on the hot infalling gas, plus the gravity-lensed light of stars behind it — bent into the famous ring.
questions.misconception: The famous photo looks like a ring of fire around a dark dot, so 'that is the hole glowing' is the easy reading — but the ring is light from outside, warped by the hole's gravity.

questions.prompt: How does a stellar black hole form?
options: A star explodes and everything in it becomes a hole instantly
The heaviest star cores collapse past the neutron-star limit (~3 solar masses) and nothing can stop it
Galaxies swallow their own centers
Old planets merge underground
questions.explanation: When a collapsing core exceeds roughly three solar masses, even neutron degeneracy pressure fails, and the collapse has no brake — it proceeds all the way to the singularity.
questions.misconception: 'Explosion' sounds like the origin, but the hole is the opposite of an explosion's debris: it is the un-stopped contraction of the leftover core after the supernova.

questions.prompt: Could our Sun ever become a black hole?
options: Yes, in about 5 billion years
No — the Sun is far too light; it will end as a white dwarf
Yes, if a black hole visits our solar system
No, because the Sun is too heavy
questions.explanation: Forming a black hole needs a collapsing core of at least ~3 solar masses. The Sun carries only one, so its future ends as a white dwarf, not a hole.
questions.misconception: Black holes feel like a normal star's future because they're famous — but the Sun's mass is far below the threshold, a point this component's mass dial makes immediate.

questions.prompt: What happens to an object falling toward a black hole?
options: It freezes instantly
Tidal forces stretch it into a long thin strand — 'spaghettification'
It bounces back like a rubber ball
It catches fire and burns away
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls harder on the near side of the object than the far side; the stretch difference is so extreme near a horizon that an astronaut is drawn out into a thread.
questions.misconception: Falling into the hole's gravity sounds like 'falling into a funnel' — but the real effect is a stretching, not a sliding: the two ends of your body get pulled apart at different strengths.
